title: Entropy: measuring surprise
summary: The surprise of an outcome with probability p is log(1/p): zero for a certain event, larger for rarer ones, and additive for independent events. Entropy is the average surprise of a distribution, H = Σ p·log(1/p). It is largest when probability is spread evenly and zero when one outcome is certain.
llm_link: Every next-token prediction of a language model is a distribution with an entropy: low when the continuation is obvious ("The capital of France is …"), high when many continuations are plausible. Cross-entropy, the training loss, is built directly from this idea (lesson 3.7).
key_ideas: Surprise(p) = log(1/p) = −log p. Certain events (p = 1) carry 0 surprise.
Independent events: probabilities multiply, surprises add (the log turns products into sums).
With log base 2 the unit is bits: a fair coin flip is 1 bit, an outcome with p = 1/8 is 3 bits.
Entropy H(p) = Σ p(x)·log(1/p(x)): the expected surprise. Uniform over n outcomes gives log₂ n bits, the maximum.
Terms with p(x) = 0 contribute 0 (they never happen).

quiz.q: Predict the result: how many bits of surprise does an outcome with probability 1/16 carry?
quiz.explain: log₂(1/(1/16)) = log₂ 16 = 4 bits, the same as four fair coin flips landing in one particular order.

quiz.q: Which distribution over four outcomes has the highest entropy?
quiz.explain: Entropy is largest when probability is spread evenly. The uniform distribution over 4 outcomes has log₂ 4 = 2 bits; [0.5, 0.5, 0, 0] has only 1 bit.

quiz.q: Two independent events happen, with surprises of 2 bits and 3 bits. What is the surprise of both happening?
quiz.explain: Their probabilities multiply (1/4 · 1/8 = 1/32), so the surprises add: log₂ 32 = 5 bits.

quiz.q: A coin lands heads with probability 1. What is its entropy?
quiz.explain: The only outcome that happens has surprise log(1/1) = 0, and the impossible outcome contributes 0 because it has probability 0. Nothing is left to learn.

quiz.q: A language model's next-token distribution after "The capital of France is" puts 0.93 on "Paris". Compared with its distribution at the start of a fresh sentence, its entropy is…
options: The same, because the vocabulary is the same
quiz.explain: A peaked distribution has low entropy. At the start of a new sentence many tokens are plausible, so the distribution is flatter and its entropy higher.

problems.title: Surprise in bits
problems.prompt:
Write surprise(p) that returns the surprise in bits, log₂(1/p). Use math.log2.

surprise(0.5)    # 1.0
surprise(1/8)    # 3.0
surprise(1.0)    # 0.0

tests.name: fair coin
tests.code:
out = surprise(0.5)
assert out is not None, 'returned None'
assert abs(out - 1.0) < 1e-12, f'a fair coin flip carries 1 bit, got {out}'

tests.name: one in eight
tests.code:
out = surprise(1/8)
assert abs(out - 3.0) < 1e-12, f'p = 1/8 is like three coin flips: 3 bits, got {out}. Check that you use log base 2'

tests.name: certain event
tests.code:
out = surprise(1.0)
assert abs(out) < 1e-12, f'a certain event has zero surprise, got {out}'

tests.name: independent surprises add
tests.code:
a, b = surprise(0.25), surprise(0.1)
assert abs(surprise(0.25 * 0.1) - (a + b)) < 1e-9, 'surprise of both events should equal the sum of the surprises'

tests.name: positive, not negative
tests.code:
out = surprise(0.2)
assert out > 0, f'surprise should be positive for p < 1, got {out}. log(1/p) = -log(p)'

problems.title: Entropy of a distribution
problems.prompt:
Write entropy(ps) = Σ p·log₂(1/p) for a list of probabilities, in bits.

Outcomes with p == 0 never happen, so they contribute 0; skip them (otherwise 1/p raises ZeroDivisionError).

entropy([0.5, 0.5])     # 1.0
entropy([1/8] * 8)      # 3.0
entropy([1.0, 0.0])     # 0.0
problems.starter:
import math

def entropy(ps):
    h = 0
    for p in ps:
        # TODO: skip p == 0, otherwise add p * log2(1/p)
        pass
    return h

tests.name: fair coin
tests.code:
out = entropy([0.5, 0.5])
assert abs(out - 1.0) < 1e-12, f'a fair coin has 1 bit of entropy, got {out}'

tests.name: uniform over 8
tests.code:
out = entropy([1/8] * 8)
assert abs(out - 3.0) < 1e-12, f'uniform over 8 outcomes gives log2(8) = 3 bits, got {out}'

tests.name: certain outcome
tests.code:
out = entropy([1.0, 0.0])
assert abs(out) < 1e-12, f'a certain outcome has zero entropy, got {out}. Are you skipping p == 0?'

tests.name: a biased coin
tests.code:
import math
out = entropy([0.9, 0.1])
exp = 0.9 * math.log2(1/0.9) + 0.1 * math.log2(10)
assert abs(out - exp) < 1e-12, f'expected {exp:.4f} bits, got {out}. Each term is p * log2(1/p): weight the surprise by its probability'

tests.name: uniform is the maximum
tests.code: assert entropy([0.25] * 4) > entropy([0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1]), 'the uniform distribution should have the highest entropy'

hints: if p > 0: h += p * math.log2(1 / p)
Or in one line: sum(p * math.log2(1 / p) for p in ps if p > 0)

problems.title: Entropy in nats with NumPy
problems.prompt:
Machine learning code usually uses the natural log, which measures information in nats (1 bit = ln 2 ≈ 0.693 nats). Write entropy_nats(p) for a NumPy array p, without a Python loop.

Use a boolean mask to keep only the positive entries: q = p[p > 0], then -(q * np.log(q)).sum().

entropy_nats(np.array([0.5, 0.5]))        # 0.6931...
entropy_nats(np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]))   # 0.0

out = entropy_nats(np.array([0.5, 0.5]))
assert out is not None, 'returned None'
assert abs(out - np.log(2)) < 1e-12, f'a fair coin has ln 2 = 0.6931 nats, got {out}'

tests.name: zeros are ignored
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out = entropy_nats(np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]))
assert abs(out) < 1e-12 and np.isfinite(out), f'a certain outcome has zero entropy, got {out}. 0 * log(0) gives nan in NumPy; mask the zeros out first'

tests.name: uniform over a vocabulary
tests.code:
import numpy as np
V = 50000
out = entropy_nats(np.full(V, 1 / V))
assert abs(out - np.log(V)) < 1e-6, f'uniform over 50000 tokens gives ln(50000) = 10.82 nats, got {out}'
